chapter: Growing up in the Thirteenth Ward
title: Music in the neighbourhood growing up
summary: Local piano players like Ape Man played by ear, and Carnival parades like the Jefferson Buzzards passed with hired Black bands.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: But I was going to say, when you were growing up as a kid, you were talking about your father playing piano. Did other people in the neighborhood play piano? Were the other piano players? Was that kind of a tradition?
Well they had a few guys around playing, but they played, you know, they all played by ear, different ones. Had a guy, his nickname was Ape Man. He played little things around there. Ape? Ape?
Yeah, Ape Man. Ape Man, yeah.

He played little things on the piano. But he couldn't play like my dad. He played like little bluesy stuff. Something like Professor Longhair. That's where Ape Man played, something similar to that. I can't think of anybody. Next door on 616 Bell Castle Street, there used to be another guy. He was almost blind. He used to play guitar. I used to hear him strumming the guitar all the time. But I never did know, I didn't know what he was playing because I wasn't very interested at the time, you know. That's about the only music that I can remember around the neighborhood. Except for Carnival Day when I, you know, see parades around the corner at the, on Chappatula, on Anteus H. Street, the Zulus, not the Zulus, I mean, they called it. The Jefferson Buzzards. The Buzzards, yeah. Yeah, the Buzzards used to be around in the block, yeah. And they'd hire black bands and they'd pass by and they had the Lion Street and they'd pass. All of them looked like they'd come from the Audubon Park going down or coming up, whichever way. But there always was music around that neighborhood, you know.
